```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
inla_available <- bdlnm::check_inla()
```

```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(bdlnm)
library(dlnm)
library(splines)
library(utils)
```

In this example, we will estimate the temperature-mortality effect for each age group, in the city of London. 

First, we have to convert the data from wide to long:

```{r}
london_age <- london |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(
    cols = c(mort_00_74, mort_75plus),
    names_to = "age",
    values_to = "mortality"
  ) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    age = gsub("mort_", "", age),
    age = factor(age)
  )
```

# Set DLNM parameters

We will start by building the crossbasis with the `dlnm` package. The crossbasis has to be built on the unique series of temperature (now we have each temperature repeated twice, one for each age group).

We will use a natural spline with three knots for the exposure–response function, placed at the 10th, 75th, and 90th percentiles of daily mean temperature, and a natural spline for the lag–response function, with knots equally spaced on the log scale up to a maximum lag of 21 days:

```{r}
# Exposure-response and lag-response spline parameters
dlnm_var <- list(
  var_prc = c(10, 75, 90),
  var_fun = "ns",
  lag_fun = "ns",
  max_lag = 21,
  lagnk = 3
)


# Cross-basis parameters
argvar <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$var_fun,
  knots = quantile(london$tmean, dlnm_var$var_prc / 100, na.rm = TRUE),
  Bound = range(london$tmean, na.rm = TRUE)
)

arglag <- list(
  fun = dlnm_var$lag_fun,
  knots = logknots(dlnm_var$max_lag, nk = dlnm_var$lagnk)
)

# Create crossbasis
london_unique <- london_age[!duplicated(london_age$date), ]
cb <- crossbasis(london_unique$tmean, lag = dlnm_var$max_lag, argvar, arglag)
cb_attrs <- attributes(cb)
cb <- rbind(cb, cb)
class(cb) <- "crossbasis"
cb_attrs$dim      <- dim(cb)
cb_attrs$dimnames <- dimnames(cb)
attributes(cb) <- cb_attrs
```

Let’s define the seasonality of the mortality time series using a natural spline with 8 degrees of freedom per year, which flexibly controls for long-term and seasonal trends in mortality:

```{r}
# Seasonality of mortality time series
seas <- ns(london$date, df = round(8 * length(london$date) / 365.25))
seas <- rbind(seas, seas)
```

Finally, we also define the temperature values for which predictions will be generated. These correspond to an evenly spaced grid with a 0.1ºC step covering the full range of observed temperatures in the data:

```{r}
# Prediction values (equidistant points)
temp <- round(seq(min(london$tmean), max(london$tmean), by = 0.1), 1)
# Ensure it falls inside the range of temperatures after rounding:
temp <- temp[temp >= min(london$tmean) & temp <= max(london$tmean)]
```

# Fit the model and posterior samples

We will fit a B-DLNM model with the effect of the crossbasis interacting with the age:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
mod <- bdlnm(
  mort ~ cb*age + factor(dow)*age + seas*age,
  data = london_age,
  family = "poisson",
  sample.arg = list(n = 1000, seed = 1L)
)

# test it works also when adding a f() in the formula
london_age$id <- seq_along(nrow(london_age))
mod <- bdlnm(
  mort ~ cb*age + factor(dow)*age + seas*age + f(id, model = "iid"),
  data = london_age,
  family = "poisson",
  sample.arg = list(n = 1000, seed = 1L)
)
```

The `bdlnm()` function runs `inla()` which correctly identifies the interaction term and expands this effect across all crossbasis coefficients. The matrix stored in `$coefficients` now contains the baseline estimated crossbasis coefficients (`cbv1.l1`, `cbv1.l2`, ...) and a coefficient for the other category in age (`cbv1.l1:age75plus`):

```{r}
DT::datatable(mod$coefficients)
```

# Predict exposure-lag-response effects

We can predict the exposure–lag–response association between temperature and mortality from the fitted model in each different `id_year` unit, specifying it with `terms`:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
tictoc::tic()
cpred <- bcrosspred(mod, combine_effects = ~ cb*age, exp_at = temp)
tictoc::toc()
```

A `bcrosspred` object is returned containing posterior samples of the estimated exposure–lag–response association for each different unit in `id_year`, and for the global:

```{r, eval = inla_available}
str(cpred, max.level = 1)
```

# Plot

## Age: 0-74

We can visualize a 3d plot:

```{r}
plot(cpred, terms = "age[reference]", ptype = "3d", main = "Age: 0-74, exposure-lag-response effect")
```

Or the overall cumulative plot:

```{r}
plot(cpred, terms = "age[reference]", ptype = "overall", main = "Age: 0-74, overall cumulative effect")
```

## Age: 75+

We can visualize a 3d plot:

```{r}
plot(cpred, terms = "age[75plus]", ptype = "3d", main = "Age: 75+, exposure-lag-response effect")
```

Or the overall cumulative plot:

```{r}
plot(cpred, terms = "age[75plus]", ptype = "overall", main = "Age: 75+, overall cumulative effect")
```
